_slice: California and Los Angeles in depth — indexation, pensions, housing allocation and the local rent formulas
_note: The second US pass, broadening the worked vertical rather than adding a second state. Four parallel research passes: California's statutory indexation machinery, the public pension chain, the Los Angeles programme layer, and housing allocation and revenue forecasting. The theme that emerged was not planned. California legislates against a great many different price indexes and almost never the same one twice: the minimum wage reads the federal CPI-W, income tax brackets and the fuel excise tax read the California CPI, welfare payments read a purpose-built California Necessities Index, property assessment reads the California CPI through a Board of Equalization letter, and rent control in the City and County of Los Angeles reads a Los Angeles metropolitan CPI — at 90 percent of it in the city and 60 percent of it in the county. Five different indexes, one state, and each choice is a policy decision hiding inside a technical citation. The pension chain is the other structure worth having: an experience study sets assumptions, the assumptions set a valuation, the valuation sets a contribution rate, and the rate lands in a budget one or two years later. It is the longest documented lag in the corpus and it runs from a mortality table to a line item.

reports.title: Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W)
reports.description: The CPI variant covering urban wage earners and clerical workers, a narrower population than the CPI-U and weighted differently. It is a separate published series and statutes name it specifically — California's minimum wage adjustment reads the US city average, not seasonally adjusted, and will not accept CPI-U in its place.

entries.covers: July 2026 CPI (CPI-U and CPI-W)
August 2026 CPI (CPI-U and CPI-W)
September 2026 CPI (CPI-U and CPI-W)
October 2026 CPI (CPI-U and CPI-W)
November 2026 CPI (CPI-U and CPI-W)

release_schedule.note: BLS publishes CPI-U and CPI-W together in a single monthly 'Consumer Price Index' news release, per the official BLS release schedule calendar at bls.gov/schedule/news_release/cpi.htm. Release time is 8:30 AM Eastern.

reports.title: Consumer Price Index, Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim
reports.publisher: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Western Information Office
reports.description: The metropolitan-area CPI-U for the Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim core based statistical area, covering Los Angeles and Orange counties. A distinct series from the national CPI-U, and the index named by name in both the City and the County of Los Angeles rent stabilization ordinances — so a federal metropolitan statistic sets the legal ceiling on rent increases for millions of tenants.

entries.covers: July 2026 CPI, Los Angeles area
August 2026 CPI, Los Angeles area
September 2026 CPI, Los Angeles area

release_schedule.note: The Western Information Office's LA-area CPI release page states the next release explicitly ("The July 2026 Consumer Price Index for the Los Angeles area is scheduled to be released on August 12, 2026"). LA is one of the few metro areas BLS publishes CPI for every month; its release date matches the national CPI release date exactly (per the BLS national CPI schedule at bls.gov/schedule/news_release/cpi.htm), so subsequent dates below are taken from that same shared calendar.

reports.title: California State Minimum Wage Rate
reports.description: The statewide minimum wage under Labor Code §1182.12. Since the $15.00 phase-in completed, the rate is adjusted annually for inflation by the Director of Finance, determined on or before August 1 and effective the following January 1, capped at 3.5 percent in any one year and never adjusted downward.

entries.covers: California state minimum wage rate effective January 1, 2027 (next annual CPI-W-based adjustment)

release_schedule.rule: After the state minimum wage reached $15 an hour, the rate is adjusted annually for inflation based on the national consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers (CPI-W). The minimum wage cannot be lowered, even if there is a negative CPI, and the highest raise allowed in any one year is 3.5 percent. New rates take effect January 1 of each year (per Labor Code section 1182.12).
release_schedule.note: The current rate of $16.90/hour took effect January 1, 2026 (already past relative to 2026-08-11), so the next expected adjustment/effective date is January 1, 2027, per the statutory annual-adjustment rule. The exact certified dollar figure for 2027 is not yet published by DIR/Department of Finance as of this research; only the January 1 effective date and the CPI-W-based, 3.5%-cap adjustment mechanism are confirmed from the publisher's own FAQ page.

reports.title: California Necessities Index (CNI)
reports.description: A statutorily defined weighted price index for food, clothing, fuel, utilities, rent and transportation for low-income consumers, computed by the Department of Finance from BLS CPI components using the area weights of the California CPI. A purpose-built poverty-basket index that exists because the general CPI was judged not to describe what a welfare recipient buys.
reports.cadence_note: Weakly anchored on purpose: the statutory duty to compute the index is clear (W&I Code §§11453, 12201) but no standing Department of Finance page publishing the series could be found, and the figure surfaces inside budget documents and county letters instead. The URL is the closest publisher landing page, not a verified index page.

entries.covers: Next statutory annual CNI-based adjustment effective date

release_schedule.rule: Welfare and Institutions Code Section 11453: annual adjustments to grants based on the California Necessities Index, computed by the Department of Finance from CPI-based cost data for food, clothing, fuel/utilities, rent, and transportation, "shall become effective July 1 of each year."
release_schedule.note: The DOF page given as the corpus URL (dof.ca.gov/forecasting/economics/economic-indicators/) does not mention the CNI at all — no calendar or CNI reference found there. Per Welf. & Inst. Code 11453, CNI-based adjustments take effect July 1 each year; July 1, 2026 has already passed as of today (2026-08-11), so the next occurrence is July 1, 2027. Note a complication found via LAO (Aug 2025, https://www.lao.ca.gov/reports/2025/5065/Updating-CA-Necessities-Index-081425.pdf): BLS discontinued publishing the specific consumer expenditure data the CNI formula relies on, making the index impossible to compute under the old formula starting with the 2026-27 budget. A 2026 budget trailer bill (Gov. Code 13074.1, see https://trailerbill.dof.ca.gov/public/trailerBill/pdf/1337) subsequently authorized DOF to use "a reasonable estimate" of missing data for such cost-of-living/annual-adjustment calculations, with the resulting calculation deemed final — which appears intended to preserve continuity of the annual July 1 CNI adjustment cycle going forward, though I found no DOF page explicitly confirming a computed CNI value for July 2027 yet.

reports.title: CalWORKs Maximum Aid Payment schedules
reports.description: The maximum monthly cash aid by assistance-unit size for CalWORKs, adjusted annually under Welfare and Institutions Code §11453 and effective each July 1.

release_schedule.note: CDSS issues an All County Letter (ACL) announcing a Maximum Aid Payment (MAP) level increase only in years the enacted state budget funds one; there is no statute or fixed calendar requiring an annual MAP increase. Confirmed MAP-increase ACLs: ACL 22-60 (issued 2022-07-20, 11% permanent + 10% temporary increase), ACL 23-74 (issued 2023-08-30, increase effective 2023-10-01), ACL 24-55 (issued 2024-08-08, MAP level increase). No MAP-increase ACL was issued in 2025 (the 2025 ACL list instead shows only a June COLA to MBSAC/income-in-kind levels via ACL 25-36, and a September resource-limit increase via ACL 25-65 -- neither is a MAP increase). As of 2026-08-11, no MAP-increase ACL has appeared in the 2026 ACL list either (latest reviewed is ACL 26-52, 2026-07-16), and the analogous 2026 COLA letter (ACL 26-39, 2026-06-12) again covers MBSAC, not MAP. Because the 2025 cycle broke the 2022-2024 pattern, this is genuinely budget-dependent/irregular rather than a fixed annual release.

reports.title: SSI/SSP Payment Standards
reports.description: Combined federal Supplemental Security Income and California State Supplementary Payment grant levels. The federal portion moves with the federal SSI cost-of-living adjustment each January; the state portion has had no automatic adjustment since 2011 and changes only when the Legislature names an amount.
reports.cadence_note: The statutory California Necessities Index adjustment in W&I Code §12201 is still on the books but suspended — no adjustment is made "unless otherwise specified by statute". The live mechanism is the federal COLA plus discretionary legislative increases.

entries.covers: Annual federal SSI COLA adjustment effective January 2027 (California combined SSI/SSP payment standard updates accordingly)

release_schedule.rule: Federal SSI benefit rates (and the California combined SSI/SSP payment standard tied to them) are adjusted annually each January via the Social Security Administration's Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA), determined by CPI-W and announced in October of the prior year (Social Security Act §1617/42 U.S.C. §1382f). California's SSP portion is additionally subject to change through the annual state budget process (Governor's Budget in January, May Revision in May), but statutory automatic CNI-based COLA increases to the state supplement have been suspended in most recent budget years.
release_schedule.note: The January 2026 COLA (2.8%) already took effect (confirmed via ssa.gov/oact/cola/SSI.html: $994/individual, $1,491/couple federal SSI as of Jan 2026), so the next occurrence is January 2027. CDSS's own SSI/SSP page (the corpus url) does not display a calendar or explicit COLA schedule directly — it links to budget documents (Governor's Budget, May Revision) and historical COLA letters, but the underlying driver (federal SSI COLA effective every January) is well-documented on ssa.gov. Could not confirm via a CDSS-specific dated publication/ACL due to robots.txt blocking cdss.ca.gov PDF/letter pages and exhaustion of the web search budget mid-task.

reports.title: Motor Vehicle Fuel, Diesel Fuel and Aviation Gasoline Excise Tax Rates
reports.publisher: California Department of Tax and Fee Administration
reports.description: Per-gallon fuel excise tax rates, adjusted every July 1 for inflation under Revenue and Taxation Code §7360(d) as enacted by SB 1 in 2017, and published by CDTFA special notice each spring.

entries.covers: Motor vehicle fuel, diesel fuel and aviation gasoline excise tax rates effective July 1, 2027 through June 30, 2028

release_schedule.rule: Revenue and Taxation Code section 7360(d) requires CDTFA to adjust the motor vehicle fuel, diesel fuel and aviation gas excise tax rates on July 1 of each year based on the percentage change in the California Consumer Price Index.
release_schedule.note: The document currently at the corpus URL (L1025.pdf) already covers rates effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027 (dated June 2026), so the next scheduled annual adjustment is July 1, 2027.

reports.title: Annual Inflation-Adjusted Personal Income Tax Schedules
reports.description: The annual indexation of personal income tax brackets, filing thresholds, the standard deduction, exemption credits and the renter's credit income limits, using a percentage change the Department of Industrial Relations is required by statute to transmit to the Franchise Tax Board by August 1 each year.

entries.covers: 2024 tax year complete rate schedules (Schedules X/Y/Z) and exemption amounts
2025 tax year complete rate schedules (Schedules X/Y/Z) and exemption amounts
2026 tax year complete rate schedules (Schedules X/Y/Z) and exemption amounts

release_schedule.note: FTB's October Tax News each year previews the CCPI-based inflation adjustment (brackets, standard deduction, exemption credits) for that tax year, and states verbatim that 'The complete [year] tax rates and exemption amounts will be available on FTB's website in late December.' Confirmed identical wording/pattern in the October 2024 and October 2025 Tax News editions (for 2024 and 2025 tax years respectively). No fixed statutory publication day was found, only this consistent late-December timing observed across at least two consecutive years, so classified as observed-pattern rather than stated-rule. The next full-year schedule (for tax year 2026) is expected in late December 2026.

reports.title: CalPERS State Actuarial Valuation
reports.description: The annual funding valuation of the State of California's CalPERS plans, determining the required state employer contribution rate and dollar amount, the funded ratio and the unfunded accrued liability. Explicitly a funding document: it carries a disclaimer that it "should not be used in financial reports subject to Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement Number 68".

entries.covers: State Actuarial Valuation as of June 30, 2022 (actuarial certification date)
State Actuarial Valuation as of June 30, 2023 (announced available via Circular Letter 200-045-24, certified July 2024)
State Actuarial Valuation as of June 30, 2024 (companion Schools Pool valuation certified September 2025)
State Actuarial Valuation as of June 30, 2025 (next expected certification/public posting, projected from observed pattern; board summary already presented April 2026)

release_schedule.note: CalPERS does not publish a release calendar or a stated statutory release date for the State Actuarial Valuation (covering State Miscellaneous, State Industrial, State Safety, POFF and CHP plans). It is produced annually with a valuation date of June 30. Observed pattern across the last several cycles: the valuation is presented in summary to the CalPERS Finance & Administration Committee the following April (e.g. the June 30, 2025 valuation results, including 79.2% funded ratio, were presented as agenda item 5d on April 14, 2026), then the full actuarial certification and the public-facing PDF report/circular-letter notice follow roughly July-November of that same year (13-17 months after the June 30 valuation date). Confirmed cycles: June 30, 2022 valuation certified October 2023; June 30, 2023 valuation certified July 2024 and announced as publicly available via Circular Letter 200-045-24 on October 14, 2024; June 30, 2024 valuation's companion Schools Pool report was certified September 2025 (State report expected on a similar timetable). As of 2026-08-11, the June 30, 2025 valuation has already been summarized to the board (April 2026) but the full certified public report had not yet appeared in search results, so its formal certification/posting is projected for roughly September-November 2026 based on the observed multi-year pattern.

reports.title: CalPERS Public Agency and Schools Annual Actuarial Valuations
reports.description: Plan-by-plan annual funding valuations issued to every participating city, county, special district and school employer, setting each one's required contribution rate and unfunded-liability payment for a fiscal year two years after the valuation date. Distributed each July with a circular letter.

entries.covers: June 30, 2022 actuarial valuation reports (circular letter 200-041-23)
June 30, 2023 actuarial valuation reports (circular letter 200-038-24)
June 30, 2024 actuarial valuation reports (circular letter 200-038-25)
June 30, 2025 actuarial valuation reports (next annual release)

release_schedule.note: CalPERS releases the annual public agency/school actuarial valuation reports (based on data as of June 30 of the prior year) to employers via myCalPERS in early-to-mid August each year, then posts them publicly on the CalPERS website by the end of September. No fixed statutory date was found; timing is inferred from three consecutive years of circular letters (200-041-23: Aug 9 2023; 200-038-24: Aug 13 2024; 200-038-25: Aug 14 2025). Circular letter 200-038-25 itself states the next valuation (June 30, 2025 data) will be 'available August 2026.' As of the research date (2026-08-11) no circular letter announcing the June 30, 2025 valuation reports had yet appeared, consistent with mid-to-late August timing.

reports.title: CalPERS Experience Study and Review of Actuarial Assumptions
reports.description: The quadrennial review of actual system experience — retirement, termination, disability, mortality, salary growth, inflation — against the current assumptions, recommending revised demographic and economic assumptions to the Board of Administration for use in every CalPERS valuation. Board policy requires one every four years.

release_schedule.rule: The report has been prepared in accordance with current board policy which requires that an actuarial experience study be performed every four years.

entries.covers: Next CalPERS Experience Study and Review of Actuarial Assumptions (following the 2025 study)

release_schedule.note: The most recent study (the 2025 CalPERS Experience Study and Review of Actuarial Assumptions, analyzing FY2000-2023 data) was presented to the Finance and Administration Committee in November 2025 and adopted for use with the June 30, 2025 actuarial valuations. Past studies were published in 2010, 2014, 2017, 2021, and 2025, consistent with the stated ~4-year board policy cycle. No official date for the next (circa-2029) study has been announced yet; 2029 is a projection based on the stated interval, not a published date.

reports.title: CalPERS GASB 68 Accounting Valuation Reports
reports.description: Accounting-basis reports giving each participating employer its proportionate net pension liability, deferred inflows and outflows, and pension expense for a stated measurement date, for inclusion in the employer's financial statements. Deliberately separate from the funding valuation — CalPERS states that GASB 68 "is an accounting change only and not related to funding".

entries.covers: GASB 68 Agent Accounting Valuation Reports, measurement date June 30, 2022
GASB 68 Schools Accounting Valuation Report, measurement date June 30, 2023
GASB 68 Agent and Cost-Sharing Accounting Valuation Reports, measurement date June 30, 2025
Projected release of GASB 68 Accounting Valuation Reports, measurement date June 30, 2026

release_schedule.note: No published release calendar exists. CalPERS announces availability of GASB 68 Accounting Valuation Reports (Agent, Cost-Sharing, and Schools versions) each year via Circular Letters roughly 7-8 months after the June 30 fiscal-year-end measurement date, consistently in the late-January to mid-February window (e.g. Jan 26 2023, Jan 29 2024, Feb 9 2026). No circular letter for the 2025 cycle (MD June 30 2024 reports) was located in this search, but the pattern otherwise holds across the years checked. Next release (for measurement date June 30, 2026) is projected for late January to mid-February 2027 based on this pattern, not a stated rule.

reports.title: CalSTRS Defined Benefit Program Actuarial Valuation
reports.description: The annual valuation of the CalSTRS Defined Benefit Program presented to the Teachers' Retirement Board each spring. Unusually, the base employer, member and state contribution rates are fixed in the Education Code rather than set actuarially: the valuation supports only a bounded board adjustment of at most 1 percent of payroll a year, to a ceiling of 20.25 percent.

entries.covers: DB Program actuarial valuation as of June 30, 2024, presented to CalSTRS Teachers' Retirement Board
DB Program actuarial valuation as of June 30, 2025 (Milliman report issued April 28, 2026), presented to Teachers' Retirement Board
DB Program actuarial valuation as of June 30, 2026 (projected next annual valuation)

release_schedule.note: CalSTRS commissions Milliman to perform an annual actuarial valuation of the Defined Benefit Program as of each June 30 fiscal year end. The written report is typically issued in April of the following year and presented to the Teachers' Retirement Board at its May meeting (e.g., May 8, 2025 board item for the 6/30/2024 valuation; May 28, 2026 board item for the 6/30/2025 valuation, Milliman report dated April 28, 2026). No published fixed calendar or statutory date was found specifying an exact release date, but the annual June 30 valuation date / spring report / May board presentation cadence has been consistent across at least the 2024-2026 cycles.

reports.title: California Population Projections (P-series)
reports.publisher: California Department of Finance, Demographic Research Unit
reports.description: Projected population by age, sex and race or ethnicity with components of change, household projections and public K-12 enrolment, for the state and every county. A separate product from the E-series estimates: the estimates say what the population is, the projections say what it will be, and the housing allocation machinery reads the projections.

entries.covers: Vintage 2025 (Baseline 2024) initial public data release
Vintage 2026 (Baseline 2024) update, reflecting latest published July 1 population estimates
Projected Vintage 2027 update

release_schedule.note: DOF's population projections page (dof.ca.gov/forecasting/demographics/projections/) uses a 'Baseline' + 'Vintage' system: a new demographic 'Baseline' (methodology/assumptions reset) is produced only every several years (previous baseline was 2019/2020-era; current is Baseline 2024), while within a baseline, 'Vintage' updates are issued to refresh figures against newer population estimates. Only two vintages exist so far under Baseline 2024: Vintage 2025 (initial release, 2025-09-30) and Vintage 2026 (update, 2026-03-13, 'Updated to reflect latest published July 1 population estimates. No change to 2024 Baseline assumptions'). This is a thin (2-point) pattern suggesting roughly one vintage update per year, consistent with the corpus's releases_per_year=1, but no explicit calendar or stated rule for the main P-series was found on the page. A separate sub-series (birth projections) does have a stated rule: 'Planned updates are scheduled for November of each year,' but that applies only to birth projections, not the main population projections series, so it was not used as the primary schedule. The projected March-2027-ish next vintage entry is a rough extrapolation from a single annual-cadence data point and should be treated as low-precision.

reports.title: Regional Housing Need Determination
reports.publisher: California Department of Housing and Community Development
reports.description: The statutory determination of how many housing units, by four income categories, each region must plan to accommodate over an eight-year housing element period. The sixth-cycle determination for the Southern California region was 1,341,827 units. Issued to each council of governments roughly two years before its housing element deadline.

entries.covers: HCD Regional Housing Need Determination (RHND) for the SCAG (Southern California) region, 7th Cycle

release_schedule.note: HCD issues a separate Regional Housing Need Determination (RHND) per council-of-governments region on a staggered, region-by-region schedule (the statewide process runs on 5-8 year statutory planning periods under Gov. Code 65584/65588, matching the corpus's 0.125/yr ≈ 1-per-8-years figure). The nearest, best-documented upcoming determination is for the Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG) region — the largest MPO region — which both SCAG's official RHNA page (scag.ca.gov/rhna) and its 7th Cycle launch announcement (scag.ca.gov/news/scag-launches-7th-cycle-rhna-process-schedule-and-subcommittee) state HCD will issue in October 2026, covering the SCAG region's 7th-cycle planning period of October 2029-October 2037. Other regions (e.g., ABAG/Bay Area, SACOG, San Diego, and numerous rural HCD-direct counties) have their own separate 7th-cycle determination dates not all consolidated in one public calendar; several rural county 7th-cycle determinations were already issued 2020-2025 (e.g., Sierra, Modoc, Mariposa, Alpine counties), and others remain due through 2027-2032 per a 7th-cycle housing-element due-date schedule (mintierharnish.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/01_7th-web-he-duedate.pdf), reflecting the report's fundamentally rolling, per-region publication pattern rather than a single nationwide release date.

reports.title: California's Fiscal Outlook
reports.description: The Legislative Analyst's independent multi-year General Fund revenue and spending projection, published each November, evaluating the budget "based on current law and policy both at the state and federal level" against the enacted Budget Act. The institutional counterweight to the executive's own forecast.

entries.covers: The 2022-23 Budget: California's Fiscal Outlook
The 2023-24 Budget: California's Fiscal Outlook
The 2024-25 Budget: California's Fiscal Outlook
The 2025-26 Budget: California's Fiscal Outlook
The 2026-27 Budget: California's Fiscal Outlook
The 2027-28 Budget: California's Fiscal Outlook (projected)

release_schedule.note: LAO states 'Each year, our office publishes the Fiscal Outlook in anticipation of the upcoming budget season,' but does not commit to a fixed calendar date. Actual publication dates over 2021-2025 cluster in mid-to-late November (one outlier: Dec 7, 2023), always ahead of the Governor's January budget proposal. Next edition (2027-28 Fiscal Outlook) is projected for November 2026 based on this consistent annual pattern; exact date not yet announced as of 2026-08-11.

reports.title: Department of Finance Revenue Estimating Exhibits
reports.publisher: California Franchise Tax Board, Economic and Statistical Research Bureau
reports.description: Semi-annual statistical exhibits of current personal income tax and corporation tax return data and trends, produced by the Franchise Tax Board for the twice-yearly revenue-estimating conferences with the Department of Finance and the Legislative Analyst's Office. The channel through which actual tax return data reaches both forecasts.

entries.covers: Fall 2026 Revenue Estimating Exhibits (semi-annual DOF/FTB revenue forecast tied to the Governor's January Budget)

release_schedule.note: FTB's Economic & Statistical Research Bureau publishes these 'Revenue Estimating Exhibits' semi-annually as 'Fall' and 'Spring' editions, timed to the two points in the year DOF/FTB/LAO meet for budget forecasting: the Fall edition accompanies the Governor's January Budget and the Spring edition accompanies the May Revision. No fixed calendar or statutory date is published; the metadata field for update frequency is literally listed as 'Irregular'. Observed past publish dates on data.ca.gov/lab.data.ca.gov: Fall 2022 -> published/updated Jan 26-30, 2023; Fall 2024 -> created Dec 13, 2024, updated Jan 28, 2025; Fall 2025 -> published Jan 13, 2026; Spring 2023 -> data first published June 15, 2023; Spring 2025 -> published May 7, 2025 (updated July 9, 2025); Spring 2026 -> published May 15, 2026 (most recent edition as of today, 2026-08-11). Given this pattern, the next edition (Fall 2026) is expected in the Dec 2026-Jan 2027 window alongside the Governor's Budget, but no exact date has been published.

reports.title: State Appropriations Limit Summary (Schedule 12A)
reports.description: The state's own Article XIII B appropriations limit, published as Schedule 12A of the Governor's Budget and updated each January 10. The state analogue of the Gann limit the price and population factors set for cities and counties, and it moves on the same per capita personal income measure.

entries.covers: Schedule 12A at 2027-28 Governor's Budget

release_schedule.rule: The Governor submits the Governor's Budget to the Legislature in January each year (per California Department of Finance); Schedule 12A (State Appropriations Limit Summary) is published as part of the Governor's Budget Summary schedules at that time.
release_schedule.note: The document itself (BS_SCH12A.pdf) carries no explicit publication date; it is labeled 'Schedule 12A AT 2026-27 GOVERNOR'S BUDGET', confirming it accompanies the annual January Governor's Budget release. The California Constitution (Art. IV, Sec. 12(a)) is widely reported elsewhere as setting a January 10 deadline for budget submission, but I could not re-verify that exact day from a live, fetchable source this session, so I used the DOF site's own 'in January' statement (month precision) rather than assert the day. The next edition would accompany the 2027-28 Governor's Budget, expected January 2027 (the 2026-27 edition currently on file was already released for the current cycle).

reports.title: LACERA Annual Pension Actuarial Valuation
reports.publisher: Los Angeles County Employees Retirement Association
reports.description: The annual funding valuation performed under §31453 of the County Employees Retirement Law of 1937, recommending employer and member contribution rates. The Board of Investments approves the rates and the County Board of Supervisors adopts them under Government Code §31454 — which is the moment an actuarial assumption becomes a line in the county budget.

entries.covers: FY2020 (June 30, 2020) Pension Actuarial Valuation, issued by Milliman
FY2021 (June 30, 2021) Pension Actuarial Valuation, issued by Milliman
FY2022 (June 30, 2022) Pension Actuarial Valuation, issued by Milliman (Board of Investments approved resulting rates March 8, 2023)
FY2024 (June 30, 2024) Pension Actuarial Valuation, issued by Milliman (Board of Investments approved resulting rates Feb 12, 2025)
FY2025 (June 30, 2025) Pension Actuarial Valuation report/rates approved by LACERA Board of Investments (Board of Supervisors adopted rates May 12, 2026)
FY2026 (June 30, 2026) Pension Actuarial Valuation - projected next release/approval window based on the recent pattern

release_schedule.note: LACERA's actuarial consultant (Milliman) prepares a valuation report annually, with a valuation date of June 30 each year (LACERA has done annual, not just triennial, valuations since a 2009 Board of Investments policy). There is no published release calendar and no single fixed publication date; the report's issuance/approval date has drifted across recent cycles, from late November (FY2020, FY2021 valuations) to February-March (FY2022, FY2024, FY2025 valuations) of the following fiscal year, likely because the report must incorporate the triennial experience-study assumptions when those are due. Downstream, the LACERA Board of Investments approves resulting contribution rates, and the LA County Board of Supervisors must approve them at least 45 days before the July 1 start of the next fiscal year. Given the observed drift, the FY2026 valuation (as of June 30, 2026) is projected for Board of Investments approval/report issuance in the January-March 2027 window, marked as implied/projected.

reports.title: LACERA Investigation of Experience
reports.publisher: Los Angeles County Employees Retirement Association
reports.description: The triennial study of LACERA's demographic and economic experience, from which the Board of Investments adopts the actuarial assumptions — including the investment return and discount rate — used in the annual valuations.

entries.covers: Triennial Investigation of Experience for the period July 1, 2025 - June 30, 2028

release_schedule.rule: Every three years, LACERA's actuarial consultant prepares an investigation of experience to review the reasonableness of the actuarial methods and economic and demographic assumptions used in the valuation (triennial investigation of experience study).
release_schedule.note: LACERA publishes a triennial Investigation of Experience covering rolling 3-year periods ending each June 30 (past editions: 2016-2019 study, 2019-2022 study, 2022-2025 study). Based on the observed historical lag, the underlying study report is typically issued 5-8 months after the period end (e.g., the 2019-2022 study was dated Jan 6, 2023; the independent actuarial review of the 2022-2025 study was dated Feb 18, 2026), so the next study (covering 2025-2028) is expected roughly Q4 2028-Q1 2029; no exact publication date has been announced.

reports.title: Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance Annual Allowable Rent Increase
reports.description: The annual percentage by which rent on a covered unit may be raised, effective July 1 to June 30. Set by formula in Los Angeles Municipal Code §151.06(D) at 90 percent of the change in the Los Angeles-area CPI, floored at 1 percent and capped at 4, and published in a newspaper of general circulation on or before May 30 each year.

entries.covers: RSO annual allowable rent increase rate for the July 1, 2027 - June 30, 2028 cycle

release_schedule.rule: The LA Housing Department publishes the RSO annual allowable rent increase percentage each year, effective July 1 through June 30 of the following year. Per LAHD: the percentage is determined by 'the Consumer Price Index (CPI) average for the twelve (12) month period ending September 30 of each year' (as of a Dec. 2025 ordinance amendment effective Feb 2, 2026, the formula is 90% of that CPI average, with a 1%-4% floor/ceiling, replacing the prior 100%-of-CPI, 3%-8% formula). The rate for the current cycle is published by LAHD in or around June, ahead of the July 1 effective date.
release_schedule.note: The rate currently in effect (July 1, 2026 - June 30, 2027) is 3%, per LAHD's rent increase calculator page and multiple secondary sources; LAHD had not yet posted an updated rate/page reflecting the new July 2026 cycle at time of research (its calculator page still showed the July 2025-June 2026 wording), so exact current-cycle figures should be reverified on the source page. The next new annual rate takes effect July 1, 2027, with publication expected around June 2027.

dependencies.basis: Labor Code §1182.12(c)(3)(A) directs the Director of Finance to calculate an adjusted minimum wage increased "by the lesser of 3.5 percent and the rate of change in the averages of the most recent July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period over the preceding July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period for the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics nonseasonally adjusted United States Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (U.S. CPI-W)". The Department of Industrial Relations confirms the practice, reporting that the Department of Finance calculated a 6.16 percent increase for July 2022 to June 2023. The statute names CPI-W specifically, so CPI-U will not do.

reference_period.stated_as: The 12-month average July 1 to June 30 against the preceding July 1 to June 30 average; determined by August 1; effective the following January 1.

dependencies.evidence_quote: by the lesser of 3.5 percent and the rate of change in the averages of the most recent July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period over the preceding July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period for the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics nonseasonally adjusted United States Consumer Price Index for Urban Wag

dependencies.basis: Welfare and Institutions Code §12201(a)(2) directs that the index be computed from "the appropriate components of the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, as published by the United States Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics", for the Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim, San Francisco-Oakland and San Diego areas plus other California areas covering at least 80 percent of recipients. The components correspond to the six statutory categories of food, clothing, fuel, utilities, rent and transportation.
dependencies.evidence_quote: the appropriate components of the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, as published by the United States Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics

dependencies.basis: Welfare and Institutions Code §12201(a)(3) requires the category price changes for each metropolitan area to be combined using "the applicable weighting factors for each area used by the Department of Industrial Relations to calculate the California Consumer Price Index (CCPI)". The Necessities Index borrows the California CPI's area-weighting structure while substituting its own statutory expenditure weights across the six necessity categories.
dependencies.evidence_quote: the applicable weighting factors for each area used by the Department of Industrial Relations to calculate the California Consumer Price Index (CCPI)

dependencies.basis: Welfare and Institutions Code §11453(a) provides that the aid amounts "shall be adjusted annually" and that "the cost-of-living adjustment shall be calculated by the Department of Finance based on the changes in the California Necessities Index, which as used in this section means the weighted average changes for food, clothing, fuel, utilities, rent, and transportation for low-income consumers". Adjusted amounts are rounded to the nearest dollar and take effect July 1.

reference_period.stated_as: The percentage change in the index over the 12 months ending with the December preceding the adjustment year; effective July 1.

dependencies.basis: The Legislative Analyst's Office records that the federal portion of the grant receives the annual federal cost-of-living adjustment each January, that "the federal COLA is based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W)", and that when that index falls the federal government holds grants flat rather than cutting them. California's published payment standards are the sum of this federally adjusted amount and the state supplement.

reference_period.stated_as: The federal cost-of-living adjustment period, applied each January.

dependencies.basis: Revenue and Taxation Code §7360(d), added by SB 1 in 2017, provides that "on July 1, 2020, and every July 1 thereafter, the board shall adjust the taxes imposed by subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) ... by increasing the taxes by a percentage amount equal to the increase in the California Consumer Price Index, as calculated by the Department of Finance with the resulting taxes rounded to the nearest one-tenth of one cent." CDTFA's own notice repeats the requirement. Recorded ambiguity: the statute attributes calculation of the California CPI to the Department of Finance, whereas the index is in fact produced by the Department of Industrial Relations, and neither the statute nor the CDTFA notices reconcile this.

reference_period.stated_as: A 12-month window running November 1 to November 1, anchored on the initial November 2017 to November 2019 period; rates effective each July 1.

dependencies.evidence_quote: on July 1, 2020, and every July 1 thereafter, the board shall adjust the taxes imposed by subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) ... by increasing the taxes by a percentage amount equal to the increase in the California Consumer Price Index, as calculated by the Department of Finance with the resulting taxe

dependencies.basis: Revenue and Taxation Code §17041(h) provides that "the California Department of Industrial Relations shall transmit annually to the Franchise Tax Board the percentage change in the California Consumer Price Index for all items from June of the prior calendar year to June of the current calendar year", reported by August 1, and directs the Franchise Tax Board to "multiply the preceding taxable year income tax brackets by the inflation adjustment factor". The Franchise Tax Board confirms the practice, reporting a 3.0 percent factor from June 2024 to June 2025 applied to brackets, filing thresholds, the standard deduction, exemption credits and the renter's credit limits.

reference_period.stated_as: June of the prior calendar year to June of the current calendar year; transmitted by August 1; applied to the following taxable year.

dependencies.evidence_quote: the California Department of Industrial Relations shall transmit annually to the Franchise Tax Board the percentage change in the California Consumer Price Index for all items from June of the prior calendar year to June of the current calendar year

dependencies.basis: The State valuation records that "On November 17, 2021, the board adopted new actuarial assumptions based on the recommendations in the 2021 CalPERS Experience Study and Review of Actuarial Assumptions", covering retirement, termination, mortality, salary increase and inflation. The experience study states its own purpose as "to review actual experience of the system in relation to the current actuarial assumptions, and to recommend changes in actuarial assumptions", for use "in actuarial valuations of plans that participate in the California Public Employees' Retirement Fund".
dependencies.evidence_quote: to review actual experience of the system in relation to the current actuarial assumptions, and to recommend changes in actuarial assumptions

dependencies.basis: The experience study states that the recommended assumptions are "for use in actuarial valuations of plans that participate in the California Public Employees' Retirement Fund (State, Schools and Public Agencies)" — the same adopted assumption set drives the public agency and schools valuations, not only the state one. The board-adopted asset allocation "supports a 6.80% discount rate, together with a price inflation assumption of 2.30%", and that single number propagates into the contribution rate of every participating city and district.

The CalPERS circular letter announcing state employer rates records that they were "approved by the California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS) Board of Administration on April 14, 2026", and carries a second table headed "Budget Act Total Contribution Rate", showing what is appropriated through the state budget on top of the actuarially required rate. It notes that "the California State Legislature may adopt higher contribution rates than shown in the table above to redirect savings resulting from increases in member contribution rates".

reference_period.stated_as: State plans carry a one-year lag: the June 30 valuation sets contributions for the fiscal year beginning the following July 1. Public agency plans carry two years.

dependencies.basis: CalPERS states that GASB 67 and 68 "changed the way pension liabilities are reported", requiring employers to report the net pension liability, the deferred outflows and inflows related to pensions, and pension expense, and that "Entry Age Normal is the only allowable actuarial cost method". It draws the funding and accounting line explicitly: "These changes won't affect the amount of contributions sent to CalPERS; GASB 68 is an accounting change only and not related to funding."
dependencies.evidence_quote: changed the way pension liabilities are reported

dependencies.basis: CalPERS issues cost-sharing accounting valuation reports for a stated measurement date, built on the same plan census and Entry Age Normal liabilities as the funding valuations but published separately, because the funding report "should not be used in financial reports subject to GASB Statement Number 68". Employers are instructed to "discuss the audit and reporting requirements of GASB 68 with your auditors".

The valuation states that its actuarial assumptions derive from the Investigation of Experience report adopted by the Board effective with that valuation date. LACERA's annual report confirms that "a system investigation of experience (also referred to as the experience study) is performed every three years", and records the 7.0 percent investment return assumption adopted in December 2022.
dependencies.evidence_quote: a system investigation of experience (also referred to as the experience study) is performed every three years

dependencies.basis: The LACERA board letter asks the County Board of Supervisors to "Adopt the revised employer and employee retirement contribution rates approved by the LACERA Board of Investments in accordance with Government Code Section 31454", based on the June 30, 2024 valuation certified by the system's actuaries, and states that "adoption of these actuarial valuation recommendations will result in an aggregate employer contribution rate decrease of 0.27% to 25.61%" — an expected increase of roughly $91 million in the County's contribution for the following fiscal year. That adopted rate is what the County's accounts then report.

reference_period.stated_as: A one-year lag: the June 30 valuation sets rates effective the following July 1.

dependencies.basis: Los Angeles Municipal Code §151.06(D) provides that rent "may be increased annually based on 90 percent of the difference between the average of the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers for All items in Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim, CA for the most recent consecutive 12-month period ending on September 30 and the average of the same index for the prior consecutive 12-month period ending on September 30". A landlord may still raise by one percent if the result is lower, and "in no event ... may an annual rent increase under this subsection exceed four percent". The ordinance names the Los Angeles-area series, not the national index.

reference_period.stated_as: The average over the 12 months ending September 30 against the average over the prior 12 months ending September 30; the result applies July 1 to June 30.

dependencies.basis: The County ordinance defines "CPI" as "the Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers of the Los Angeles area (Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim) or any successor designation", and permits an increase of "sixty percent (60%) of the percentage change in the average CPI over the previous 12-month period ending in September, not to exceed a maximum Rent increase of three percent (3%)". The allowable increase "shall be calculated annually by the Department".

reference_period.stated_as: The average index over the 12-month period ending in September.

dependencies.evidence_quote: the Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers of the Los Angeles area (Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim) or any successor designation

dependencies.basis: The ordinance imposing the county half-cent tax provides that "Prior to the operative date, the County shall contract with the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration to perform all functions incident to the administration and operation of this transactions and use tax Ordinance", and repeals the predecessor quarter-cent measure. CDTFA's district tax listing carries both rates and their operative dates. The special revenue fund whose audits are this node is funded from those state-collected receipts.

Metro states that Propositions A and C, Measure R and Measure M "are four one-half cent sales tax measures approved by Los Angeles County voters", with fixed shares of each earmarked for local return and distributed monthly per capita. The Measure M ordinance provides that "Metro shall contract with the Board of Equalization to perform all functions incident to the administration and operation of this Ordinance" — the function CDTFA now performs — and CDTFA's district tax listing carries all four as county district taxes.

The county property tax portal describes the chain end to end: assessed values are "placed on a list with all other properties in Los Angeles County and this list is called the 'Assessment Roll'"; the Auditor-Controller "adds direct assessments to the Assessment Roll then applies the tax rates", producing the extended roll; and "The Extended Roll is then sent to the Los Angeles County Treasurer and Tax Collector for individual tax bill distribution and payment collection."

reference_period.stated_as: The roll for the fiscal year beginning July 1, valued as of the January 1 lien date; bills mailed each October.

dependencies.basis: The Auditor-Controller states that its office "computes/calculates the amount of taxes due" and "apportions and distributes to the various entities the property tax monies collected by the Treasurer & Tax Collector". The apportionment therefore takes the Tax Collector's receipts as its input, running in the opposite direction to the roll that produced the bills.

The City's report states that the statements were "prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) prescribed for governmental entities", with an unmodified auditor's opinion, and documents specific adoption: "effective July 1, 2024, the City adopted the provisions of Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences", with a $144.4 million cumulative adjustment to beginning net position.

Government Code §65584.01(a) provides that the determination "shall be based upon population projections produced by the Department of Finance and regional population forecasts used in preparing regional transportation plans". Where the regional forecast differs from the state projection by more than 1.5 percent and no agreement is reached, "the population projection for the region prepared by the Department of Finance" governs. Determination letters implement this by anchoring on a dated projection and applying the Department's household formation rates.

reference_period.stated_as: A single dated projection for the end of the eight-year planning period, adjusted forward to the housing element deadline.

dependencies.basis: The determination letters name the American Community Survey as an input alongside the state projections. The sixth-cycle Southern California letter cites "2013-2017 5-year American Community Survey (ACS) data" for vacancy and overcrowding rates; the seventh-cycle letters cite "2019-2023 5-year American Community Survey (ACS) data" and 2023 Public Use Microdata Sample data. Government Code §65584.01(b) correspondingly requires the determination to account for overcrowding, vacancy, household size and cost burden.

The association states that it "received a regional housing needs determination (RHND) from HCD of 1,341,827 housing units" and that it "is responsible for developing a methodology to allocate that need among jurisdictions within the region" — its 197 cities and counties. Government Code §65584.04(a) requires the council of governments to develop that methodology at least two years before the scheduled housing element revision.
dependencies.evidence_quote: received a regional housing needs determination (RHND) from HCD of 1,341,827 housing units

dependencies.basis: The final allocation methodology states that the jurisdiction-level projections underlying the allocation incorporate "California Department of Finance (DOF) population and household estimates", together with state employment data and Census and American Community Survey inputs. Note that the methodology names the estimates series generically rather than the E-1 table specifically.

The same methodology lists among the inputs to its jurisdiction-level projections "2010 Census and the latest ACS data (2013-2017 5-year samples)", which feed the bottom-up local input process from which household growth by jurisdiction is derived.

The official dataset description states that the Franchise Tax Board's "Economic & Statistical Research Bureau, uses the information collected to provide statistical analyses of current tax return data and trends when it meets twice a year with the Department of Finance (DOF) and Legislative Analyst Office (LAO). They use the data to assist the Governor's office in California with budget-forecasting purposes."

reference_period.stated_as: Semi-annual exhibits, feeding the January Governor's Budget and the May Revision revenue estimates.

dependencies.basis: The same dataset description names the Legislative Analyst's Office explicitly as a participant in the twice-yearly revenue-estimating meetings at which the exhibits' analyses of current return data and trends are used for budget forecasting. The independent forecast and the executive forecast read the same underlying return data, which is worth knowing when they disagree.

The Department lists "Schedule 12A: State Appropriations Limit Summary" among the budget summary schedules published as part of the Governor's Budget Summary and "updated each January 10 with the release of the Governor's Budget". The schedule derives total appropriations subject to limitation from the Governor's Budget revenue and expenditure estimates.
dependencies.evidence_quote: updated each January 10 with the release of the Governor's Budget

dependencies.basis: The Legislative Analyst's explainer of the limit states that the Department of Finance "has the responsibility for executing these calculations" and that the cost-of-living component of the growth factor is "California fourth quarter personal income, as measured by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, divided by (2) the civilian population of the state, as measured by DOF". Caveat: the documenting source is the Legislative Analyst describing the constitutional formula, not a Department of Finance publication naming the federal bureau.

reference_period.stated_as: California fourth-quarter personal income per capita, year over year.

_dropped.why: A negative finding, deliberately kept. None of the eight water adjustment factors (WSCA, WQIA, BRRTA, OVRA, LISA, WIA, WESA) or the power factors (ECA/VEA, CRPSEA/VRPSEA, RCA/IRCA, ESA) is tied to a CPI or to any external published index. Each is a cost-recovery pass-through against LADWP's own budgeted and actual expenditures, approved by the Board of Water and Power Commissioners. BRRTA specifically "recovers any shortage in revenue from Base Rates or credits back any excess collection of revenue from Base Rates due to variation in water sales from projections" — an internal variance, not an index. Checked the water factors page, the electric rate ordinance and the Office of Public Accountability rate guides. Worth recording because a utility rate escalator is exactly the kind of thing everyone assumes is indexed.

Statutory but suspended, so recorded as an observation rather than a missing input. Welfare and Institutions Code §12201(a) still provides that the payment schedules "shall be adjusted annually to reflect any increases or decreases in the cost of living" measured by the California Necessities Index, and under that mechanism the state supplement topped up whatever the federal adjustment left short. But the same section now provides that no adjustment shall be made "unless otherwise specified by statute", the automatic adjustment having been eliminated in 2011, with increases since set as specific dollar amounts. A live edge would assert a mechanism that has not operated in fifteen years. Filed as a note rather than a caveat because a caveat annotates an edge that exists, and this one deliberately does not.

The valuation names Milliman's 2024 Experience Analysis as the source of its updated assumptions, exactly as the CalPERS and LACERA valuations name theirs. No directly retrievable CalSTRS URL for the report itself was found, so the node was not minted. The CalPERS and LACERA equivalents are both in the graph, so this is a gap in a pattern rather than an absence of one.

No document found stating that teacher pension contribution rates feed into or are transmitted through the Principal Apportionment. Districts pay CalSTRS from general funds; the apportionment neither sets nor carries the rate. Recorded because the link looks obvious and is not there.

The funding valuation actively disclaims this use: it "should not be used in financial reports subject to Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement Number 68". The defensible path from pension numbers into a government financial statement runs through the separate GASB 68 accounting reports, which is why those are their own node. A rare case of a document telling you which edge NOT to draw.

The City report's management discussion says property tax revenue rose "$153.0 million, or 5.2%, driven by the growth in the taxable assessed value of properties", but the notes to the financial statements — where the standard "levied and collected by the County of Los Angeles on behalf of the City" language and the lien date would appear — were beyond the reachable portion of the PDF. Plausible, unevidenced.

The Metro budget book states that Metro projects sales tax revenue using "an economic sector model, regression analysis, long and short-term historical receipts, and leading professional financial forecasting sources like the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and Beacon Economics". This was only reachable through a third-party mirror; the official copies sit behind Dropbox links that block automated fetch. Not recorded until an official metro.net URL is confirmed.

_dropped.edge: ca-dof-california-necessities-index -> a published Department of Finance series
_dropped.why: The statutory duty to compute the index is unambiguous, but no standing Department of Finance page publishing the series could be found — the Economic Indicators page lists labour force, income, construction permits, inflation, trade and gross state product, and does not mention it. The figure surfaces inside budget documents and county letters. So a number that sets welfare payments for a million people has no home page.

The November outlook predates the January Governor's Budget and names only the enacted Budget Act as its baseline. Searches of the report text for the Department of Finance, population, Census, BEA and BLS returned nothing. The independent forecast appears to be genuinely independent of the executive's document, which is the finding.

The price and population letters are addressed to local fiscal officers under Government Code §7901 for city, county and special district limits. Nothing found ties that letter to the state's own limit, and Schedule 12A shows no price factor or population change line, even though both limits move on the same underlying measure.

The Legislative Analyst states that the Department of Social Services also uses the California Necessities Index to adjust foster care provider rates. The underlying statute (likely Welfare and Institutions Code §11461) and its measurement period were not verified, so no node or edge was created. A third consumer of the index would be worth having.

_status: NEW 2026-08-10, second US pass. Every edge carries an evidence_url. 11 candidate edges declined, including two denials — LADWP rate factors read no index at all, and the CalPERS funding valuation explicitly forbids its use in GASB 68 financial reporting.
